lines.text: A rainforest older than mankind, a colony built on sugar and slavery, an empire, a republic and a democracy. This is the story of Brazil.
Long before any people, about fifty-five million years ago, tropical forest already covered the Amazon basin. Today most of the world's largest rainforest lies in Brazil.
In April 1500, a Portuguese fleet under Pedro Alvares Cabral, bound for India, reached this coast instead, and claimed it for Portugal.
So began three centuries of colonial Brazil, where sugar and later gold were worked by forced labour.
Millions of enslaved Africans were shipped across the Atlantic to Brazil's plantations and mines, more than to anywhere else in the Americas.
In 1554, Jesuit priests founded Sao Paulo. Coffee, industry and immigration would one day make it the biggest city in the Southern Hemisphere.
A decade later the Portuguese founded Rio de Janeiro on a dazzling bay. It would serve as Brazil's capital until 1960.
By the 1700s, Portuguese street games before Lent had taken root in Rio, the beginnings of what became its famous carnival.
In 1798, a prince named Pedro was born in Portugal. He would grow up in Brazil and become its first emperor.
In 1807, with Napoleon's army closing in, the Portuguese royal family fled Lisbon for Rio, which became the capital of their empire.
When the king went home, Pedro stayed, and in 1822 Brazil became an independent country.
In September of that year, Pedro declared independence, and was soon crowned emperor, though fighting with Portuguese forces lasted into 1824.
So Brazil became an empire, one of the very few monarchies in the Americas, and it would last for nearly seventy years.
In 1831 the throne passed to Pedro the second, still a child. He reigned for almost sixty years, until a coup sent him into exile.
In Rio, the grandson of freed slaves, Machado de Assis, wrote ironic novels like Dom Casmurro that made him the country's greatest writer.
From 1864, Brazil fought alongside Argentina and Uruguay against Paraguay, a long war that left Paraguay devastated.
Alberto Santos-Dumont, a Brazilian pioneer of flight, steered airships around Paris and made the first public aeroplane flight in Europe.
Getulio Vargas, born in 1882, would dominate Brazilian politics for decades, building industry and labour laws under an authoritarian hand.
In 1888, Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law, ending slavery. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to do so.
Barely a year later, Marshal Deodoro da Fonseca led a military coup, and the empire gave way to a republic.
Oscar Niemeyer would shape Brazil in curved concrete, designing the great buildings of a new capital and working past a hundred.
In 1913, Candido Rondon and Theodore Roosevelt set off down an unmapped Amazon tributary, the River of Doubt, and barely survived the hunger and illness.
A year later, Brazil's national football team played for the first time. Its yellow shirts would win the World Cup five times.
In 1931, Christ the Redeemer opened his arms over Rio from the top of Corcovado, soon a symbol of the whole country.
Pele, born in 1940, would become football's great star, winning the World Cup three times with Brazil.
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a union leader, would help found the Workers' Party and later lead Brazil in two separate eras.
Dilma Rousseff, an economist and former guerrilla, would become Brazil's first woman president, before being impeached in 2016.
For the 1950 World Cup, Rio built the Maracana, a stadium that would hold nearly two hundred thousand people.
But in the deciding match, Uruguay beat the hosts in front of that vast crowd. Brazilians still call it the Maracanazo.
Jair Bolsonaro, a future army captain born in 1955, would rise to lead Brazil from the far right, and later be convicted of plotting a coup.
In 1958 came redemption: in Sweden, a seventeen-year-old Pele scored in the final, and Brazil won its first World Cup.
That same year, bossa nova drifted out of Rio, a soft blend of samba and cool jazz that soon charmed the world.
Ayrton Senna would win three Formula One titles, and his death in a crash in 1994 brought the country to mourning.
In 1960, Brazil moved its capital to Brasilia, a city built from nothing in the interior to the plans of Costa and Niemeyer.
Then in 1964 the army seized power. For twenty-one years it ruled with censorship and torture, while the economy grew fast but unequally.
Even so, in 1970, Pele's Brazil won a third World Cup in Mexico, with a team many still rank as the greatest ever.
After military rule ended, the new constitution of 1988 restored direct elections and promised broad social rights.
In 1994, a new currency, the real, finally tamed years of runaway inflation.
Brazil hosted the World Cup again in 2014, but suffered a stunning seven to one defeat to Germany in the semi-final.
The following year, the mosquito-borne Zika virus spread fast through Brazil and was linked to birth defects, becoming a global emergency.
In 2016, Rio de Janeiro held the first Olympic Games ever staged in South America.
Then the COVID-19 pandemic swept the world, and Brazil was among the countries hit hardest.
In January 2023, a week after Lula returned to office, Bolsonaro's supporters stormed and wrecked Congress, the Supreme Court and the presidential palace.
And in 2025, the world came to Belem, on the edge of the Amazon, for the United Nations climate summit.
From Cabral's landfall to a climate summit in the rainforest, Brazil's story is still being written.
